chapter: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
title: What black musicians said about pay inequality
summary: He says white musicians felt entitled to more and black musicians were glad to work.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, how did the musicians feel now, all of these musicians that we've mentioned, the Fletcher Hendersons, the Buster Baileys, when all of a sudden they heard that Benny Goodman was the King of Swing? You never got together and talked about that?
Well, the public decided -
Not the public, the musicians.

No, not too much. Musicians don't talk about music much, very few, very few musicians. What I mean, the ones that I talked to. I don't about the others but the ones that I talk to, we don't talk that much about music. Sit around and gossip and have a taste and call it a day.
But things like that never came up, came up like about some of the inequalities, say that for instance that here is
Benny Goodman or Glenn Miller making all of this money. How come we don't make that kind of money?
How come who don't make it?
Some of the black musicians? Or were they making just as much as the white musicians?

Brother, that's a million dollar question, because they're white and we're Negro and they just feel that they are supposed to and we are climbing now. In 10 years from today Negros will be making as much money as the whites.
But what did they say then?
Then - they just figured that the white man was supposed to make more money than the Negroes.
The musicians felt that?
The white musicians.
But how about the black musicians?
They didn't think it. They were glad to get what they could.
Why?
Why? Because they wanted to work.
It was that bad?
They weren't that bad; they were that good.
I'm saying the times were so bad that they would work for a certain amount of money that somebody wouldn't say -
Times weren't bad then. That's when times were good. Times are bad now. (LAUGHTER)
